overview: Mbyá Guaraní is a living Indigenous identity across Paraguay, Argentina, Brazil, and neighboring areas. It belongs within wider Guaraní relationships without erasing Ñandeva or Avá, Kaiowá or Paĩ Tavyterã, or other peoples. Mbyá accounts link tekoá, places where a way of life can be made, with families, forest, gardens, water, movement, words, and ceremony. Nhandereko names more than a quaint custom: a Mbyá scholar explains it as a living system of ethics and law. The atlas gives the exact id mbya one approximate 1492-1500 polygon, spanning a huge area and overlapping other labels. Those eight years are map coverage, not the dates when Mbyá people began or ended. Its 1500 disappearance is a software repaint. The eight short periods below are editorial reading windows; no event is claimed for an individual year. Regional archaeology can illuminate cultivation, pottery, and settlements but cannot automatically identify Mbyá ancestors from a sherd. Modern community studies show knowledge and political action today, never an unchanged snapshot of 1492. Mbyá language, kin relations, land defense, and creative work continue.

periods.title: A map label appears
periods.summary: The atlas first draws mbya as one broad polygon in 1492. This is an editorial snapshot, not a founding record. Archaeologists describe varied Guarani-associated material across the region, yet a pottery pattern cannot alone identify a particular Mbyá community or establish one political border.

periods.title: Read the forest carefully
periods.summary: This one-year slice has no documented Mbyá event attached to it. Contemporary Mbyá communities explain why forest, water, cultivated ground, and spiritual relations matter together. Those accounts offer necessary perspective, but their specific present arrangements must not be projected unchanged into a sixteenth-century household.

periods.title: Cultivation as a question
periods.summary: The atlas polygon remains identical throughout its eight-year interval. Guarani archaeological sites and present Mbyá cultivation invite study of crops, clearing, storage, and seed movement. Neither kind of evidence supplies a dated 1494 harvest for all places inside the polygon; this heading frames a question.

periods.title: Networks across places
periods.summary: No atlas file records a journey in this year. Study of two Misiones Mbyá communities follows different people’s pathways through forests to gather valued resources. It supports attention to movement and individual skill while leaving the exact routes and participants of the 1490s undocumented.

periods.title: A household is not a state
periods.summary: The imported coverage ledger calls mbya a state, but Paraguay records a Mbyá council of elders proposing its own cultural project. We cannot turn a present council into one centralized government over the colored region, nor impose a state model on earlier communities. This period frames a question about local authority.

periods.title: Words, music, and learning
periods.summary: There is no surviving lesson plan dated to 1497 for the exact polygon. Studies with modern Mbyá communities document teaching through speaking, singing, participation, and children’s play. These are living educational practices, useful for avoiding a school-only definition of learning, not a transcript of this particular year.

periods.title: Care and evidence limits
periods.summary: The atlas has no medical register for this year. Paraguayan ethnomedicine research documents knowledge held by Mbyá and, separately, Paĩ Tavyterã specialists, with participant validation. That evidence establishes present expertise; it cannot supply a named healer, remedy, dose, or patient in 1498.

periods.title: The software seam
periods.summary: At 1500 the exact mbya feature vanishes; sampled locations are broadly relabeled. The next 1530 snapshot keeps the new paint. No source records an accompanying Mbyá disappearance, conquest, or collective move. The eight-year slice closes only the atlas feature, while specific communities’ histories continue beyond it.

sections.title: Read the map without making it a state

items.text: The exact mbya id appears in just one of fifty audited border snapshots. Its 1492 polygon has one ring and eighty-three decoded positions, stretching far beyond any securely documented single community. The atlas calls the entry a state, but the geometry supplies no constitution, ruler, tax system, or surveyed Mbyá frontier.

The polygon overlaps labels for broader Guarani territory, Ñandeva or Avá, Kaingang, and other peoples at tested places. It directly shares TopoJSON arcs with Puri and a broader Guarani feature. Arcs are excellent drawing instructions and dreadful witnesses to treaties, ancestry, government, or family life.

The imported one-sentence summary names living Mbyá across several countries, while the map paints only a large southern region. Neither is a community-approved boundary. The coverage registry still has a missing card, and the runtime card index contains no exact mbya entry before this packet.

The preceding 1400 snapshot has no exact mbya feature, yet its absence cannot date the emergence of Mbyá identity. The missing-card register lists no staged draft, and the researched-overrides file has no correction. These gaps describe this software collection, not an empty landscape before Europeans arrived.

At the 1500 seam the target disappears and many sample points receive a broad hunter-gatherer label; the 1530 control retains that repaint. The replacement category is an atlas decision, not a credible ethnic successor. People, language, gardens, and relations do not vanish because a database changes colors.

sections.title: Make a tekoá and govern relationships

items.text: A tekoá is understood through conditions for living together, rather than only a dot on a state map. Brazil’s Mbyá language inventory records numerous named villages and their communal spaces. These contemporary locations show the need for local evidence; their coordinates cannot be copied backward to place a 1492 household.

Itaxim near Paraty formed through a recent territorial return, and its opy is a spiritual and community center. The case illustrates how land, gathering, and worship are joined in one named place. It does not prove every Mbyá village had the same layout, building material, or leadership in 1492.

At Tenondé Porã, recent Mbyá land returns involve new villages, gardens, and decisions about living together. An ethnography describes renewal and differences within that territory. Its collective work demonstrates political agency without appointing one ruler for every Mbyá community, much less for the atlas polygon in 1492.

A council of Mbyá elders in Paraguay proposed a cultural and spiritual center in 2019. That is evidence of present planning and collective authority by named people, not a template for a fifteenth-century council. The proposal also reminds map readers that governance includes what communities choose to remember and teach.

Research on southwest Misiones traces Mbyá territorial change since the 1970s. It treats places as made through particular histories, rather than fixed points inherited unchanged from an atlas. Modern movement may answer pressure, kin needs, and opportunity; the study cannot assign an identical cause to every earlier move.

sections.title: Know forests, water, and other beings

items.text: UNESCO describes living Mbyá communities in Paraguay’s Upper Paraná forest as maintaining practical and spiritual forest relations. The reserve also faces modern industrial agriculture and forest loss. This gives a named contemporary setting for ecological knowledge; neither UNESCO designation nor today’s surviving forest line maps the woods of 1492.

In two Misiones communities, researchers followed individual paths to gather medicinal plants and other resources. Their study emphasizes differing personal knowledge rather than one trail prescribed for all. Paths are real work in a landscape, yet an observed twenty-first-century route cannot be inked onto the atlas polygon centuries earlier.

Paraguay’s Indigenous community atlas records Mbyá households at Pastoreo collecting wild foods, fishing, growing crops, and using springs or wells in the 2002 census. These local figures cannot define every Mbyá household or establish water technology in an undated sixteenth-century village. The atlas was published in 2004.

Mbyá growers in São Paulo have restored juçara palms after severe extraction and cultivated trees in nurseries. That work joins food and ecological repair. It is an achievement by present communities facing a recent damaged landscape, rather than evidence that the same plantation project existed inside the atlas’s 1492 outline.

Students and educators at Tekoa Marangatu published a bilingual book in 2014 about nature, food, crafts, and medicinal plants, thanking elders who contributed. It makes Mbyá knowledge visible in community writing. The booklet’s local voices deserve their own date and authorship, without being turned into timeless folklore.

sections.title: Grow, gather, cook, and share food

items.text: A São Paulo Mbyá farming project documented multiple traditional maize varieties and the Avaxi Nhemongarai ceremony. Crops are biological, social, and spiritual work together. This modern account guides questions about seeds and cultivation, but it cannot certify fourteen varieties or a precisely dated ritual in every 1490s settlement.

The 2002 census of Pastoreo in Paraguay lists maize, cassava, sweet potato, and other cultivated foods alongside gathering and fishing. Its household percentages describe one surveyed community, not a fixed precolonial diet. Cooking and food sharing surely happened; exact recipes, quantities, and seasonal menus need narrower evidence.

The Guarani-associated Itapiranga site yielded fish, reptiles, birds, and mammals, with many bones burned or broken by people. These remains permit local questions about food and disposal beside the Uruguay River. They do not carry an ethnic tag naming every cook or prove Mbyá meals across the atlas map.

Kerexu Martim’s 2023 film follows Mbyá maize planting and harvest at Kalipety in São Paulo. A camera directed from within the community documents present care and restoration, including the meaning of seed work to its participants. It is modern history in its own right, not archival footage of 1492.

Organic residue analysis of Guarani-associated pots on Brazil’s southern coast found maize signals more prominent than aquatic foods in sampled vessels. This regional result illuminates cooking and cultivation before colonial rule. It cannot name Mbyá makers, describe every household meal, or extend automatically to Paraguay and Misiones.

sections.title: Make objects, music, and ritual space

items.text: Mbyá and Kaingang communities in southern Brazil have researched and renewed pottery making, comparing methods across villages. Funai describes clay collection, shaping, firing, storytelling, and income. Shared technique does not collapse the peoples into one identity, and a twenty-first-century renewal should not be mistaken for an unbroken unchanged workshop.

Women at Tekoa Pyau organized beadwork teaching and plans for sales and exhibitions. Their craft is skilled labor and a route to autonomy, as well as an expressive practice. Imported beads and contemporary markets are part of this story; placing identical materials in a 1492 house would be guesswork.

A study of Mbyá children describes music and play as occasions when young people learn and teach. Songs are more than museum performances; they shape daily relations. The observed children, instruments, and school setting belong to their documented time, so this does not supply the playlist of a 1490s tekoá.

Mbyá elders in Caaguazú sought a center for spirituality and culture. Their proposal demonstrates deliberation about how ceremony may be shared and protected today. The opy in named communities likewise serves collective life. Specific prayers, access rules, and ritual roles are not recoverable from a generic colored border.

Five Mbyá teachers in Araça’i helped revise a school project around knowledge taught in the opy and community. Their work joins oral practice with written planning. It is an educational accomplishment under present institutions, not proof that late fifteenth-century children sat in the same kind of classroom.

sections.title: Travel, exchange, and trade without a single capital

items.text: Misiones researchers found that paths to plants and hunting places were shaped by particular Mbyá people’s knowledge and choices. Movement can be part of ordinary work, rather than proof that a home has been abandoned. The documented paths belong to two studied communities, and no atlas boundary fixes every family’s route.

Mbyá territorial processes in Argentina have shifted with political and land pressures since the 1970s. A study of southwest Misiones makes those changes local and dated. The continuity of travel cannot license an invented 1495 migration arrow, nor does crossing a later national border erase kin and community obligations.

Modern Mbyá farmers use storage, transport, tools, and markets while tending valued seeds. Funai describes support for maize growers and ecological restoration around São Paulo. Trade and reciprocity have different forms and dates; this case demonstrates agency in a contemporary economy, not a fifteenth-century commodity price list.

Paraguay’s language office distinguishes Mbyá from other Indigenous Guarani languages and notes contact with Paraguayan Guarani and Spanish. People can exchange words and goods without becoming the same people. Present multilingualism is evidence of relationships, while the atlas’s overlapping colors cannot measure a 1490s conversation or bargain.

A modern Mbyá film and community school books circulate beyond their home settlements. That is cultural movement through screens, classrooms, and print, directed by living makers. It extends the meaning of exchange beyond material goods while keeping twentieth- and twenty-first-century technology out of the atlas’s narrow historical interval.

sections.title: Live in families and teach children

items.text: Students at Itaty in Santa Catarina published research about community life in 2014. Their school described early classes conducted in Guarani and later bilingual learning, with elders’ knowledge also moving through the opy. That is a dated local educational choice, not evidence of a uniform school system across Mbyá communities.

Fortín Mbororé in Misiones has a secondary school inside the Mbyá community that explicitly pursues intercultural education and autonomy. Its students study a modern curriculum on their own territory. This achievement counters the notion that Indigenous learning belongs only to the past, while saying nothing definite about 1492 classroom buildings.

A Paraguayan study of the Mbyá Ñevanga Renda school documents learning materials in Mbyá, Paraguayan Guarani, and Spanish. Those are three classroom languages, not interchangeable spellings of one voice. Children negotiate different public settings while retaining community knowledge; the documented project belongs to a present urbanized context.

Funai describes Mbyá children learning their mother tongue in schools on the Tenondé Porã land near São Paulo. Language work also happens with parents, grandparents, songs, and gatherings. That combination is current community action; we lack a roster of children, households, or teachers for any particular settlement in 1492.

Research centered on Mbyá women in São Paulo traces their work sustaining and changing nhandereko. Women are historical actors, not a silent category tucked behind male leaders. Family roles vary by person and place, and no modern interview can furnish a universal marriage rule or labor chart for 1492.

sections.title: Care for bodies, water, and shared places

items.text: Paraguayan ethnomedicine research on Mbyá and Paĩ Tavyterã medicinal plants was checked with knowledge holders, including spiritual leaders and traditional practitioners. The two peoples’ expertise should remain separately attributed. A plant list is not a safe prescription, and it cannot identify treatment, dosage, or illness inside the 1492 polygon.

Mbyá women health agents in Misiones took part in reproductive health training in 2017; a named community in Paraguay received clinical, prenatal, and vaccination services in 2024. These records show negotiation with modern care systems. Neither should be recast as an ancient practice or as the whole of Mbyá medicine.

A university water project at Ita Piru in Misiones worked with a Mbyá community to use springs for supply and distribution. Access to clean water requires design and labor. The case has a local date and modern equipment; no sixteenth-century pipe network follows from its existence.

A Brazilian Guarani birth cohort, mostly Mbyá and Ñandeva, found varied present housing, water, toilets, and rubbish collection. Because it combines peoples and communities, its statistics cannot be pasted onto all Mbyá. For 1492, neither the atlas nor cited archaeology locates refuse disposal or a dedicated latrine.

Mbyá residents at Jaraguá Kwaray Djekupe and partners have pursued a recent sanitation project in São Paulo. Toilets and water systems are material questions and rights today. The project does not establish an ancient bathroom design; the map has recovered no toilet, sewer, or rule about where anyone went.

The map’s 1492 start evokes European invasion, but it documents no local Mbyá encounter in that calendar year. Later missions, state borders, land seizures, and forest destruction affected Guarani histories unevenly. Scholarship on Mbyá lives around São Miguel makes colonial memory specific rather than treating every mission resident as automatically Mbyá.

Paraguayan agencies discussed Makutinga’s Mbyá land claim in 2019; another government notice records regularization for Y’akareta in Caaguazú. These named cases show how state paperwork and community territory meet in distinct processes. Neither makes the atlas outline a legal deed or turns every Mbyá place into one claim.

Mbyá communities in São Paulo marked progress on nine land demarcations in 2026. Their organizing and the state process are dated achievements, even though declaration is one stage of regularization. Land defense continues beyond the map’s 1500 endpoint; no community needs an invented fall and rebirth to have a history.

An ethnography of Tenondé Porã describes recent new Mbyá villages, renewed cultivation, and collective land returns. These are varied decisions under present pressure, rather than a single old settlement pattern. Calling all movement wandering would miss deliberate political and ecological work; calling every new plot ancient would also overreach.

The Santa Catarina museum presents Guarani-associated archaeological places, while southern research warns that the archaeological category itself was constructed from diverse regional records. Neither an excavated vessel nor a colonial mission roster automatically names Mbyá ancestors. This is a limit on attribution, not a claim that people lack deep history.

Written sample: Kerexu Martim titled her 2023 Mbyá film “Aguyjevete avaxi’i.” A university discussion glosses a closely spelled spoken form as a wish of strength to the maize. This is a contextual English rendering, not a literal dictionary translation; spelling varies, and it represents Kalipety today, not 1492 speech.

The Brazilian inventory reports strong Mbyá home-language transmission in surveyed villages and contemporary writing, while warning that villages differ. This matters more than a claim of frozen purity: children, teachers, and elders use language amid Portuguese and Spanish institutions. The inventory’s figures are sampled present conditions, not a precolonial census.

A linguistic study analyzed narratives written by nine Mbyá speakers in Paraná between 1976 and 2002. Its authors explicitly warn that these texts may not represent speech or other Mbyá varieties. The archive is precious evidence of named writers and linguistic structure, yet cannot speak for all Guarani peoples.

Research in Misiones examines Mbyá vitality, contact, variation, and language attitudes. Work with Mbyá participants also treats song, speech, observation, and writing as intertwined knowledge practices. Paraguayan Guarani, Avá, Kaiowá, and Mbyá are related but distinct; an official spelling from one cannot simply replace another community’s words.

Mbyá makers now restore seed diversity, produce ceramics and films, teach children, and lead territorial campaigns. These are achievements in changing circumstances, not museum demonstrations of an untouched past. A card ending at 1500 cannot end the communities; the atlas can close its file while people keep making new records.

ending.text: At 1500 the atlas replaces its mbya polygon, but that map seam does not end Mbyá history. Present communities defend land, publish school books, and make films. Their work continues beyond this file; the card asserts no conqueror, fall, or successor.
